In Genoa she called on Mgr Magnasco. She was received with extreme coldness and left standing while she reported on the Institute. She suffered and offered her anguish to the Father. She found the Genoa Houses in good order. With the help of Providence all is well. She has just received a consoling letter from him.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Allow me to address a word to You to give vent to my poor soul. A few hours ago I again called on Monsignor Magnasco, Archbishop of Genoa, having arrived in his Diocese only a day ago. My God! The way he received me was such that I thought I would faint; I cannot describe the manner in which he spoke to me; what an impression it made on me! My breast was under the anvil, such was my apprehension on hearing it; I said to myself: those Holy Cardinals, those Prelates, who in their humility always received this servant of the Lord with such Charity and kindness, which gave me strength to sustain so many battles; and while I felt myself fainting from having to stand the whole time reporting to him, I was not even told to sit down, though I was truly fainting; indeed I tried to finish quickly so that there would be no scene.

2. Your Most Reverend Excellency knows how much I dislike making the least scene. Patience; at once I made an offering of it to my Eternal Father and, full of resignation and peace, I clung to Jesus.

3. Forgive me if my outpouring is too bold; but to whom can I turn, having no one now but Your Most Reverend Excellency?

I also venture to ask Your advice on how I should proceed in writing to Monsignor Vitelleschi.

4. Here the Houses are doing very well, everything is in order, and Providence too keeps coming. What a consolation: I have just received a letter from You, a true balm for this wretched Servant of Yours.1 May God reward You and fill You with graces.

5. Carlottina, who is here, together with Sr. A. Vincenza, the Superior of this house and the whole Community, ask You to request a special blessing for them from His Eminence, adding Your own, and all prostrate implore from God the grace of a good journey for You.2

May Your blessing descend in a special way on this Your

most humble Servant Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The letter of 21 March 72 is consoling in every respect. But above all one calm and persuasive phrase softens the Mother's deep sorrow over the Rule: "It seems to me that this pending matter will soon be concluded, and well, with the Lord's help".

2 He had written that he and Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli would leave for Ferrara on the evening of 25 March.

They will talk better about "that person" in person. She had not accepted the postulant mentioned. She urges care over laundry and cleanliness. They must take care to hand over personal linen to Sisters who are transferred. She will send two letters, for the sisters in Via della Morte and at the Mother House respectively. She will stay in Genoa for Easter. She should look after her health. Various instructions for the house.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My Franceschina for ever

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter about that person. Don't think it is so; I don't believe it; I think the order's affairs being settled has changed him. Well, we will talk about this in person.1

2. My dear, these lines I write you I take from my eyes, because I have had to talk all day. I am tired; my stomach aches.

3. I hear too what you say about that postulant. Know that I had already sent her away, telling Signora Scopesi, who had proposed her, that I could not accept her because she had been with the Sisters of Charity, and our Constitutions require this of us.2

4. As for Clotilde, I quite think that, for the money involved, a paper will suffice without having her make a will.3

5. I urge you to have our laundry done after Easter, and the girls' too, if they need it again.4 For charity's sake, watch over cleanliness, and let nothing be wasted.

6. Here they complain that the numbers on the chemises are not those of the sisters who came, and the same with other linen.5 For charity's sake, let the Sisters' things be numbered, and when one has to go elsewhere let her be given them. This is the wardrobe-keeper's job.

7. I hope the money has reached you. I want to make you laugh: as soon as I arrived I had to empty my pocket and was left with only a few pennies.

8. I hope tomorrow to write the letters for the Sisters and will send them to you, one for that house and the other for the Morte.6

9. My dear, I am spending Easter in this little house, which seems to me the only one in which to stay buried,7 as I have no head for attending any services, so many are the tasks of every kind in this work. My God, it is my sins that stifle me. Have them pray; I hope the girls will be happy and pray more fervently.

10. You ask me about the visit to the Holy Sepulchre;8 they could go at times when no one is there, but it will be much better if they do as in other years, when they stayed at home.

11. I hope you received the letter in which I told you about Monsignor's reception of me.9

12. I enclose two lines for you-know-who, but I want them handed to him by you and no longer sent through Giovanni. You know that on Wednesdays he goes to St Joseph's; you can have him called and give it to him, and so save yourself going to S. Lazzaro. I am not writing the address; you know whom it is for.10

13. For charity's sake, take care of yourself, don't overwork, keep calm, for this poor Mother of yours always holds you close in the heart of Jesus; for charity's sake, think of your health; I will send you pills, by tomorrow I hope; take them and you will recover completely. You see, my dear, when we no longer have our health we are good for nothing.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you; believe me always your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

14. God bless all; let them pray. Of Caroli-

na's11 things we kept no record, because she kept them herself, and as everything

gets sorted out, she had them given back when she returned; so we never had much

of them. It will be good for the girls to stay indoors all day;

it is better, for charity's sake. I wouldn't know what to tell her about dairy foods; let her ask Don Piacenza.12 Let her never refuse any postulant if she does not have 500 F. on entry and 3000 F. dowry; so I mean that whoever wishes may come, whoever doesn't may stay.

Yes, sweets at recreation and coffee; the rest you know;13 if [you have] not yet sent the basket, I would need a crucifix and the rosaries I left.

1 This refers to Fr Tornatore. As the letter referred to and any

other information on the matter are missing, nothing more precise can be known.

2 The Marchioness Laura Anguissola Scopesi had proposed a postulant,

but the Mother had already told her that under the Rule she could not be accepted,

being a former Daughter of Charity. Cf. L 201, 1.

3 Sr. A. Clotilde Rognoni was to collect a modest sum

from her relatives.

4 After Easter, i.e. after 31 March.

5 The Sisters' personal linen was marked.

6 These are the following letters: 197 (in part) and 198.

7 In the nursing sisters' house at Via S. Maria di Castello 8, Genoa.

8 Visit to the Holy Sepulchre, as is still customary on Holy Thursday.

9 This is L 194 of 23 March.

10 She was to hand the letter to Fr Tornatore personally and not through

the gardener, taking advantage of his visit to St Joseph's church on

Wednesdays.

11 Carolina's things, cf. L 187, 3.

12 Don Pietro Piacenza was chaplain of the Mother House.

13 For Easter the Sisters were to be given sweets and coffee during re-

creation.

At last she has had news from the House, four days after her arrival. She had been worried by the silence. She herself had been unable to write for serious health reasons. She addresses all the Sisters, urging trust in their Superiors. Their conduct towards them should be marked by sincerity and simplicity. They should practise mortification, above all of the tongue and of thoughts, and strive to cultivate their vocation and look on high.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter,

1. Today I received your letter enclosing the Milan programme, as well as the good news from the Mayor and from Grandi.2 Let us bless the Lord that, in these times when poor Religious are so harshly treated, they tolerate the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate.

2. I am also very sorry at the sad news of my good daughter Benedetta. Patience! If it so pleases the Lord, let us too savour his pleasure, so that every drink becomes sweet to us, even one made of gall.

3. I was really worried because I had no news of you; today it was 4 days since I left, and I had not a single line from you. You will know why I did not write to you at

once; Father will have told you: I could barely put two lines together two days after arriving here, because the journey was truly wretched and the next day brought an even greater strain; I was seized by pains all over my body so dreadful that they made me faint. Today I can barely breathe a little, and still not well.

4. How is the good postulant in charge of the middle girls? For charity's sake, look after her, for she is a miracle; poor thing, seeing her so resigned edified me.

5. Have you sent Sr. A. Concetta's things yet? If by chance they are still to be sent, put in one of the girls' plates.3

6. Now let us come to you.4 Tell me: why do you make together all those silly resolutions, whispering in each other's ears, saying things that do your souls no good, being contrary to perfection and to your Rule?

7. It says: you shall be of one heart with your Superiors; you shall long for your Superiors to share fully in all your secrets, and you shall be glad every time you are corrected.5

8. Instead, here are your concerns and the whispering you have been doing these days: oh, we must be careful not to talk to the Mother, or rather watch how we talk, seeking every means to hide each of your actions from me and from Father, and many other things I have no time to put down now.

9. Tell me, our daughter, is it true?6 You see that this poor Mother of yours knows your affairs even from here.

10. Believe me, my blessed daughter, this way of behaving makes you lose all trust in your Superiors, who stand in the place of God.

11. Truly, I never gained so much trust in my Superior as when he reproved me and rebuked me for my faults.

12. With you it is quite the opposite: as soon as you are reproved and corrected, you lose trust at once and look for ways to hide from their eyes. Tell me, is it true?7

13. Come, stop puffing yourselves up with all your silly notions. Be simpler, and so you will always have the white feathers of the dove, and the black feathers of the crow will never grow on you.

14. Have pity on your soul, which you keep locked in the prison of your body. It weeps because it is in the house of its

spouse and cannot enjoy him, nor even taste his delights, because you continually let it die, or rather languish for hunger of good works, of mortifications; the first are those of the tongue, and then those of the thoughts, driving them away, especially when they are against the Superiors; others are those of the palate, others those desires for worldly happiness that often cross your minds, others are to think little of your vocation and of the great grace God has given you.8 What do you think? Ah! Daughter, you who see so short a way, try to see far, and then your gaze will be on high and never on the low things of earth.9 Greet Sr. A. Vincenza for me; I will write to her soon; and for Carlotta I enclose a line here; pray much. Goodbye; the Lord bless you; I am your

poor MOTHER ROSA

P.S. Maria is much better; today the Countess came to see me with Vincenza's note.10

1 Neither the addressee nor the date is noted in the draft. They are inferred

from internal and external context.

2 The letter being answered is missing. One may suppose that from Milan Don Eliseo

Ghislandi (cf. Letters 1, p. 523) [had written] about the proposal to open a House of the

FSA. Cf. AFSA, 96, GhlM.

3 Sr. A. Concetta Vernengo. Un tondo: a plate for the girls.

4 She now addresses the Sisters of the Mother House community directly.

5 The underlining is M. Rosa's, but she does not quote verbatim the Rule of '69, which

devotes Chapter 11 to this subject.

6 Tell me, our daughter... my blessed daughter, in the singular because she wants

to touch the hearts of those at fault.

7 This invitation to dialogue is a subtle teaching device.

8 She urges them to "make their calling and election ever more sure" (cf. 2 Pet

1:10), pointing out the faults to correct in order to free themselves from "deceitful

passions and be renewed in holiness" (cf. Eph 4:20-24).

9 "Seek the things that are above... set your minds on things above, not on things of the

earth" (Col 3:1-2). St Paul's strong and dense warning fits well with M. Rosa's exhortation,

poetically expressed in the image of a gaze directed

upwards.

10 Maria D'Annenkoff (cf. L 14, n. 6) and her mother, Countess Vera Berz.

Having been unable to speak to them before leaving, she warns them to be careful in speech. They should not make suppositions about a remark heard from the Superior, nor turn it into gossip. They should put into practice the advice received and the Rule on how to behave with confessors, and value their learned and upright confessor. They should not go out walking, should love one another and pray.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughters

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Being unable to say anything to you before I left about your fine way of acting and so many invented devilries, contrary as they are to your Rule and to what your Superiors have taught you.1

2. I cannot think what spirit has taken hold of you; I can only tell you that I would never have imagined that you, having misunderstood a remark of the Delegate Francesca, would use it as material for an ugly plot, confiding a thousand invented rumours to one another.2

3. Hellish tongue, better that you were always still than let loose in talk like this.3

4. I understand everything, and I do not intend this letter for all of you, only for those who know they have done what I wrote above.

5. Many times your Superiors have taught you how you should make your confession, and first of all they told you that to confessors you must tell your sins and, besides, whatever you need for your spirit, because your Rule commands this; all the more when we have confessors as upright and learned as Signor Defilippi,4 who by God's mercy truly guides us to perfection.

6. I will not dwell longer on this, because I want to touch briefly on another point. My God! It was never heard of that the poor Daughters of Saint Anne go out walking in threes! Horror! What ugly things, what thoughtlessness is this?5 Ah! How often the Holy Mother must have wept!

7. Try to make amends for the great harm done, and now that you are so few, love one another, and let charity accompany you in all your actions. Pray that God may send providence, and always believe me

Your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 The sentence is left unfinished. It should be completed: I am writing to you now. Fine way, in

an ironic sense. The sisters did not trust their Superior and, fearing that

the Mother would find out, lived in fear, imagining who knows what pun-

ishments. Cf. L of Sr. A. Francesca Camisa n.d. - AFSA, F24, 1.

2 The Superior, Sr. A. Francesca, had advised some sisters of that

community to turn to the Mother, as the Rule prescribes.

3 St James warns against intemperance of the tongue: "It can poi-

son the whole body, drawing its flame from Gehenna" (Jas 3:6).

4 Giuseppe Defilippi, of the Priests of the Mission, was the ordinary confessor

of the Community. On conduct with Confessors cf. L 139, n. 2.

5 out walking in threes. She uses irony to make the rebuke effective.

Two Sisters were supposed to go and teach catechism in the Parish. Instead of

going at their appointed time, they waited for the third, who was

to go later. Cf. L Francesca Camisa cited above in n. 1.

She tells her she wants to make a change in the house. So she is sending Sr. A. Vincenza; she should receive her as if she were the Mother herself and leave her free to act, and in this way she will not tire herself. She hopes she will find no difficulty in changing rooms; she will be glad when she hears the reasons.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today, after you left, I arranged several things for that house;1 and since I cannot come myself, I am sending Sr. A. Vincenza. She will tell you my wishes, and, as if it were I myself, give her freedom to act as I have instructed her; in this way you will not tire yourself so much, as these are all tiring tasks.2

2. I hope you will have no difficulty in changing rooms, as Sr. A. Vincenza will explain; I know how much you love your house and its good — I have had abundant proof of it — and this change is being made for its good; I am sure that when you hear the why and wherefore you will be filled with joy.

3. Meanwhile try to arrange your room upstairs properly, as Sr. A. Vincenza will tell you; so on my arrival everything will be in order and we can spend a few hours together. We will talk about the affairs of that house. I add nothing more; everything in person. Goodbye. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 The Superior had come from Sampierdarena to Genoa, where the Mother was

staying for a time. After she left, M. Rosa thought it well

to make some changes in the house.

2 Among other things, some furniture was to be moved from one floor to another.

With great regret she must tell her that she has spent more than all the other houses, although she has the subsidy and a well-furnished house. For this reason she must take care to save and avoid household expenses. She should be extremely prudent, not speak about Father Tornatore, and look after the school.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter and ours

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter with the account; I very much regret having to tell you that you have spent more than all the other houses: you are 12 Religious, and in 6 months [you have spent more] than those here in Genoa, who are 15. They spent 1000 F. in a year, and you in six months. My God! What are those household expenses? When you had everything! Alas! How shall we carry on?

2. Ah! Squarzoni was unfortunately right when he complained to me.1 For pity's sake, consider that it will be a very serious matter for this poor Mother of yours. On every side I am pierced by thorns in every way.

3. S. P. D'Arena, for food, 4000 F. — with 40 girls. For pity's sake, watch what you do;2 I don't know which way to turn. In short, as for household expenses, I mean that you should not spend even a cent, and for food, with the bread you have and other things too, you must economize; well, you must see to it.3

4. Here and in all the other houses we live meagrely, and you must do the same there.

5. Be patient, my dear daughter. You know, at the Casa del Verme,4 in these months, with 32 Religious, they spent a third of what you did. See whether I am right. Try to economize, otherwise it is a serious matter.

6. For Easter, sweets at recreation with coffee, one extra dish at dinner and fruit; that is what we do here.5

7. Moreover, I want you to say nothing to the friar in answer to what he asks you about that person. For charity's sake, nothing to anyone; that is my wish.6

8. As for Sr. A. Carmelina,7 I fear she has a tapeworm; say nothing to her; if so, I will treat her when I come.

9. For now I have nothing more to tell you, except, for charity's sake, to look after the schools, so that they go well and are satisfied; so they can truly see that they are being taught.8 God bless you. I want this letter to be taken as a daughter should hear a Mother's reproofs, and not as punishment and displeasure. I will say no more. I am ever your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. Greet everyone for me; to you and all I wish the choicest blessings.

1 Giuseppe Squarzoni, Countess Maria Anna Trotti's steward, had

made some remarks about the expenses.

2 osserva che fai = pay close attention to spending.

3 In short... I don't want her to spend even a cent

on "household expenses", etc. They had the subsidy in money and also a cer-

tain quantity of food and bread.

4 At the Mother House, in the former Palazzo Dal Verme.

5 Cf. L 196, n. 13.

6 That is, about Fr Tornatore. She is to reveal to no one the decisions of the ecclesiastical

authorities concerning him. Cf. L 171, 1.

7 Sr. A. Carmelina Caretta had been unwell for some time. Cf. Lett. of

Adelaide Pezzoni, March 1872, to M. Rosa.

8 That they may see that they are being given an education.

How to proceed regarding the acceptance of two postulants. She should send off the three Sisters, notifying her by telegram. She should send Sr. A. Concetta's things. Instructions about home nursing and the girls. She should arrange two beds as directed.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter in which you again mention the postulant who was a Sister of Charity. For charity's sake, don't take her any more, don't accept her; have her told that you cannot for now, but will give her an answer in a fortnight.1 As for the one with 1000 (a thousand) Fr., you could have told her to come and present herself; and then you will accept her if she is strong [and] has a thousand francs at once; but the one who was a "cappellona", that is, a Sister of Charity, [no]. I hope you have understood me.

2. I cannot understand why you will give nothing to Sr. A. Apanasia's mother.2 I will come. I note the bills you have paid; you did well; send me the receipt for the basket so I can collect it.

3. Send me Sr. A. M. Cristina, Sr. A. Filomena and Sr. A. Felicita.3 When you send them, telegraph me, so that it doesn't happen as it did last time.

4. As for separating at that Lady's house: listen, don't you know that in a case like this they may separate?4 So tell her they should separate and let the maid sleep, and one should stay

with the patient while the other goes to make the broth. I hope that person has already suggested this to you. Send all Sr. A. Concetta's things; that way you can ship them together with those of the three other Religious.5

5. As for little Pagani, it is a grace that her father should take her; yes, give her to him; it is a grace. I repeat, for charity's sake, take good care not to accept the Ruspigiani girl; no, always no.6

6. It would be good if you had that curtained bed in the guest quarters, where I used to sleep — or rather where Carlotta slept — put in your room; put it in your room so there will be two curtained beds, which will be better; and there put Sr. A. Vincenza's bedstead with our straw mattress, since everything now on that bed is what you will take to your room.7 Put all Sr. A. Vincenza's things there; I think I have made myself clear.

7. Carlotta will send you a letter for that person; get it to him at once; if you'd rather not go yourself — and I fear the exertion may harm you — you can send it, telling Giovanni to be sure to hand it to him personally.8 Goodbye; the Lord bless you and all the others; believe me your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 Cf. L 196, n. 2.

2 The mother of Sr. A. Panasia Bellardi.

3 Sr. A. Cristina Carrara, Sr. A. Filomena Re, Sr. A. Felicita Ghisleri.

4 As to her question whether the two nursing sisters may se-

parate while nursing a lady, she thinks that in the case put

to her they may. Cf. Rule of '69, Chap. 8, pars. 6 and 16.

5 Sr. A. Concetta Vernengo.

6 Little Teresa Pagani, sister of Ermelinda, who died in the Institute on 12

March 1872. The Ruspigiani girl, surely a girl asking to be admitted among

the "pericolanti".

7 Lo scafo: the bedstead.

8 ...the letter for Fr Tornatore, ...you can entrust it to Giovanni (the gardener),

telling him to deliver it directly to the addressee.

She has sent her a letter for Fr Tornatore without telling her how important it is. She should reply whether she received it. She should tell him to write a letter to Adelaide Vernengo. She has received the basket. She is waiting for a document. She should send the money to the Superior at Sampierdarena.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I had another letter from you, and I sent you one in a wrapper; I was in such a hurry that I had no time to send you these two lines. My dear daughter, for pity's sake, reply at once whether the letter reached you and whether you sent it on to its destination, into his very hands. My God! Until I have your reply I cannot rest for fear that someone may have read it. My God! I keep saying: what if Franceschina thinks it unimportant and sends it to him without a word, or has it left in someone else's hands! You know, cepinetto puts so many ideas into my head; write to me at once.

2. I am glad to hear about Teresina. Poor Father Agostino!1 Dear, take care of yourself, and this summer we must try to make arrangements for her to be admitted to the baths.

3. Let us hope that, if you have paid the bills, you will also pay the miller.

4. You ask me to pray for your father,2 and I already have, but my prayers are worth little; you have proof of that.

5. Tell that person to write a couple of lines to the Vernengo sisters, especially to the one who is not yet a Religious.3 He can do this, for she needs encouragement — not for the sake of money, but let him speak to her of God, that it is His will, that they have done right, as I am convinced. See that he writes these lines and then gives them to you to address, and address it here to Genoa, to Sr. A. Concetta, as you know.

6. Today we received the basket with everything you said would be in it; but it is not worth sending meat, because the carriage costs more than the goods.

Greet everyone for me, and receive my wish for heavenly blessings, as I remain your

poor MOTHER [ROSA GATTORNO]

7. I am waiting for the papers from Merli, who never sends them, so every-

thing drags on; I wish he would hurry and send them. Do me the

kindness, if you can, of sending the money to the Superior at S. P. D'Are-

na, who really needs it; if you can — I cannot give it.

1 The girl Teresina Ferrari. There is no further information to identify her,

nor about her connection with Fr Agostino Donadio.

2 Sr. A. Francesca's father had been in bed "for more than twenty days"; her

mother had told her on 27.3.72. (Cf. AFSA, F24, 4).

3 To the Vernengo sisters (cf. L 177, n. 7). The one not yet a religious is Ade-

laide. She received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 19 May 1872 and took the name

Sr. A. Giuseppa; the other, Luigia, had gone before her. Her clothing had taken place

on 7 July 1870, and she had taken the name Sr. A. Concetta.

The sisters have arrived safely; she should carry on calmly; she has done everything well. She should insist that the Secretary pay, because, contrary to what he says, he can afford it. Let us hope providence comes; have them pray. For firewood she should call on the Marchioness Landi. She will not be able to return so soon; she must go to Nizza.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I could not write to you today as soon as the sisters arrived,1 because I was busy all day and Sr. A. Vincenza is at S. P. D'Arena. My dear, you cannot imagine how overwhelmed with work I am.

2. So the sisters arrived quite safely; I have read your letter and heard all that you are doing; everything is fine; and also that, while waiting, you are afraid I may turn up unexpectedly. Be of good heart; that does not even cross my mind.

3. Don't believe Secretary Parmigiani, because that is how he talks, but I know he can pay; he has the habit of complaining; don't give in; let him pay — make him pay, for he can. He always complains, and yet I know he has money.2

4. Let us hope providence comes; I hope so; you will see that more will come. Don't lose trust, for charity's sake; have them pray, for by prayer everything is obtained. Jesus, our Good, will bestow his treasures on us. Courage, patience! We shall have all we desire.3

5. For firewood, call on the Marchioness Landi and on the lady

who lives in her Palace, the Vigolesi; you will see that between the two of them they will send you some; indeed the Marchioness Landi had promised me a cartload.4 Go and ask her to send it, for Saint Anne will multiply it for us.

6. I enclose two lines for you-know-who.5

7. Listen, you say I shall come soon; who knows how long I shall have to stay here. I fear I must spend next week here too, and then I shall have to stop in Nizza for a few days. You see, my dear daughter. It is late, my eyes are burning; I close by wishing you every good from God; I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

8. I commend to you the letter enclosed in this one;

for charity's sake, see that it reaches its destination safely. It would be good for you to act

as sacristan, so as not to tire yourself so much, you and Sr.

A. of the Good Shepherd, [or,] I hardly know, Sr. A. Elisa-

betta; but don't give her the big keys, only those of the small

sacristy, because she can act as assistant wardrobe-keeper and junior sacris-

tan;6 all this, however, only if you think fit.

1 Cf. L 201, 3.

2 Secretary Parmigiani had had two daughters at the House of Saint Anne

since November 1869. The Mother insists that he pay the fees. These were small: 75 L.

a quarter for both (cf. receipt book, AFSA).

3 Do not mistrust Jesus' word: "Ask and it will be given you... knock and

it will be opened to you, for everyone who asks receives... to the one who knocks it will be opened" (Mt 7:7-8).

Do not lose heart; strengthen your heart in perseverance, for we shall have everything...

4 The Marchioness Teresa Landi and the other, the Marchioness Vigolesi.

5 For Fr Tornatore.

6 It would be good for you to act as sacristan and, so as not to tire yourself too much, Sr.

A. of the Good Shepherd Bastia or Sr. A. Elisabetta Veronesi (I don't know myself which

to choose) can serve as assistant wardrobe-keeper and assistant sacristan.

She should have Sr. A. Carmelina seen by a doctor. She should send her 300 francs, as she needs money to conclude a deal requiring considerable expense. Provision for the school. They should pray that another postulant enters, as able as the one at Sampierdarena.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. A line, though late: it is nearly 2 after midnight. Today I received your letter about Sr. A. Carmelina. You can have her examined; her illness is already known, but it is good to call the doctor, and you can ask Monsignor which one to call.1

2. Another thing I have long wanted to write to you is that you should manage to see Ferri and tell him that it would be good to invite Countess Trotti to be president of his Congregation; do you understand me?2

3. Another thing. I would like you to send me at once 300 F. by money order or registered letter, asking at the post office which is safer, as I have a big deal to make. Pray that it goes well. Have them pray that I may soon conclude it, that is, close the contract, for then it will be a great benefit for the Daughters of Saint Anne; but the costs of the deeds require a lot of money.3 I am taking it from everywhere I know it is to be had.

4. When I come, everything in person. This is what is delaying

my coming; I need so many things. Pray, and send me this money quickly, quickly.

5. I will see to the schools; here with us I have a dear postulant teacher like the one at Nizza, who will soon take our habit. What a dear creature! I am almost sorry she is here teaching boys.4

6. If the Lord sent me another, even one a little less able, I would bring her with me to Ferrara; truly an angel. Dear, pray as hard as you can that another may come to me; then I will bring her to you. All the Religious love her dearly; she deserves it.

7. So now you know why I am delayed, and the main reason is money, because for this deal it is 1000 F. to the Government, and then I shall have one of 400 for the lawyers; so I am going everywhere, but so far I am still far off.

8. Goodbye; I am sleepy, or rather my stomach aches. This evening Sr. A. Vincenza is away at S. P. D'Arena. God bless you; believe me always your

affectionate MOTHER ROSA

God bless all the others. Silence about what I am writing, silence; for charity's sake, speak of it to no one.

1 In her letter of 1 April the sister had told her of the complaints of

Sr. A. Carmelina Caretta and asked whether she should call the doctor and ask

Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist which one.

2 The Parish Priest Gaetano Ferri wanted to found the Congregation of Chris-

tian Mothers. Cf. L 131, 1.

3 The deed concerned the Casa Dal Verme in Piacenza, specifically the can-

cellation of the mortgages in the relevant notarial deeds. Cf. L of 30 May 1872 from secre-

tary Merli to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino. AFSA. Mother House Piacenza.

4 A dear postulant teacher. In all probability Adelaide Campidel-

li. She took the religious habit in the Sampierdarena House on 19 May 1872.

Petition for authorization to hold a lottery.

Your Excellency,

1. Taking advantage of Your kind disposition,1 and of the endless kindnesses Your Excellency has continually shown to me and our poor house, I beg You to add one more, much needed by me: to use Your influence with the Government2 so that we may obtain permission to begin our lottery, which Your Excellency will know has been set up for the benefit of our poor little girls, as I am sure that one word from You will obtain everything for us.

2. I also beg You to give the bearer of this letter Your consent to distribute the tickets while the permit is awaited.

3. Your great charity, which I have experienced whenever I have turned to You, gives me hope that You will not refuse me this favour, for which I venture to thank You in advance, assuring You of my keen gratitude, which I shall always keep towards Your Excellency, as I sign myself with the most distinguished esteem and respect Your Excellency's

[most humble and obliged ROSA GATTORNO]3

1 kindly offers.

2 with the government authorities.

3 The autograph draft omits addressee, date and signature, which are

however given in a copy transcribed by the first secretary, Sr. A. Vincen-

za Rapallino. Cf. AFSA, M1Q6.

She explains how to speak to the father of a girl whom he wants to withdraw from the Institute. She sends her medicines. She advises her how to deal with a sick girl.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. If that wretched father comes, say these words to him, reading him the letter; indeed, send for him: "You want your daughter, and I promise you that before the month is out you will have her; but know that men of honour do not behave like this. You say you will do something wicked and you care little if they put you in prison; well, I tell you that a Christian should not be frightened by prison but by the justice of God, which is the only thing you must fear. When your daughter comes, you will see to taking her away, for we no longer wish to bother with it; so you will learn how to behave, a man without heart or head. Come at the end of this [month] and you will have your daughter".1

2. I want to know whether that Person is in Piacenza or away, and what day he will arrive.

3. A trunk will reach you, and inside you will find the pills for you and the plaster for Eufemia;2 they should take good care of it and put it only on Eufemia, and tell her to have faith when putting it on, for if she has faith she will be cured. Look after yourself, take the pills, the foot baths for three days, and do whatever you think best.

3. See whether, in the case of the Ferrari girl,3 you could arrange for her to die outside the house. Send for those who placed her with us and ask them to take her back, and once they have her they can put her in hospital. You can tell these people to see whether fresh air outside might do her good, for she would need it. Try, and then you will see. I will say no more. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER R. God bless you; I am yours

1 The wretched father is Signor Albano Carmeli, whose daughter, one of the first

admitted to the Mother House, precisely on 11 October 1876, at the time of the cholera,

wished to become a religious and was spending her postulancy in the House at

Ferrara. Cf. L 153, n. 2. In her letter to M. Rosa of 11.4.1872 Sr. A. Francesca had

mentioned this gentleman's threats and unreasonable intentions.

2 ...the plaster for Sr. A. Eufemia Mirisola; but it was a remedy effective only

if used with great faith.

3 Delfina Ferrari, aged 16, was very ill. "She is getting into a bad state, the doctor said so

yesterday", Sr. A. Francesca had written the day before. She did in-

deed die on 10 May 1872. Cf. L 233, 1.

She was edified by the way the little girls pray and no longer doubts their future, for with the weapon of prayer every enemy is overcome. She should look after her postulant. She asks her to give her greetings to the sisters.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I am writing two little things I ask you to do; one is that you will find enclosed 2 fr., which are for buying me a lamp like yours, and if this letter arrives in time, send it with Don Luigi,2 who will kindly bring it to me.

2. Have your dear little girls pray, for they edified me; I will tell you more: when I speak of it I cannot help being moved, so much so that my eyes fill with tears.

3. Ah! I no longer doubt your future, for you will have all you desire; with this weapon every enemy is overcome. Prayer is powerful; it opens the gates of Paradise; so take courage.

4. My daughter, I commend to you your postulant Adelaide; she must be a little flower of your garden, that is, of your labours; the Holy Mother will reward you.3

5. Look after your health; try to eat properly and not to overwork.

6. Tell Sr. A. Angiola that I understood nothing of her note, and that it would have done for a prophetess, but not for me, a wretched creature.4

7. You will have heard how our Holy Mother Saint Anne answered us by sending a teacher. Tell Don Luigi to arrange for her to come soon, so that we can do what I told you.5

8. Greet Signora Morando for me and tell her I always think of her; greet all the sisters and the Vernengos too; tell Sr. A. Concetta that as soon as I have a minute I will write to her.6

9. I am on my feet, but my bones are all in a bundle; I hope Adelaide has received a letter from me.7 God bless you and your whole Community; believe me your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 The addressee, not given, is easily identified from the date and con-

text.

2 Don Luigi Decavi, director of the Institute at Sampierdarena. Cf. Letters 1,

p. 521.

3 Adelaide Campidelli. She received the religious habit on 19 May 1872.

4 Sr. A. M. Angiola Degrossi. She had written her a mysterious note, intelli-

gible to a "prophetess", not to her.

5 Don Luigi Decavi had played an important part in opening the

house at Nizza Monferrato. AFSA, Casa Nizza Monferrato.

6 Signora Nina Morando, faithful benefactress of the Sisters of the Community

at Sampierdarena. For the Vernengos cf. L 177, n. 7.

7 The postulant mentioned above.

For pity's sake, she must look after herself. She will be in Piacenza on Tuesday. She hears of the bread debt. She doesn't know what to say; she hasn't a cent.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Just one line. I have your letter and hear of your poor health. For pity's sake, look after yourself, go to bed earlier, and think about having mustard plasters1 put on and whatever you think good for the blood.

2. On Tuesday2 I shall be at Piacenza station with the 10 a.m. train; I cannot come earlier. Please get this letter to that Person as soon as you can; tell him I wrote that I shall arrive on Tuesday at 10.

3. Be of good heart; you tell me the baker wants to be paid; I don't know what to say, because I haven't a cent. This time there were too many debts at S. P. D'Arena; they amounted to 3000 F. What do you think? They made me sweat enough. God will help us.3

4. Be cheerful, for soon I will tell you everything in person. I close so that this goes before noon. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER

1 Senapismi: poultices of mustard flour.

2 Tuesday 16 April. That person: Fr Tornatore.

3 I haven't a cent, ...God will help us. In broken, sparse

phrases she expresses the heavy reality of poverty to be faced. With courage, ingenuity

and toil she managed to free the Sampierdarena work from heavy debt and saw

the hand of providence at work. Her trust in God's help knows

no cracks and grows ever stronger.

She apologizes for her delay in giving thanks for the subsidy granted to the "pericolanti". The cause was her long absence.

Most Illustrious Director,

1. I beg Your Illustrious Lordship's pardon a thousand times for not having fulfilled earlier my duty of thanking You for the subsidy You sent for our poor pericolanti. The reason was that I had been away from the city for a long time.

2. As soon as I returned I hastened to do so, hoping that in Your kindness You will grant me gracious pardon and now accept my warmest thanks, together with the request that You continue Your benevolence to this poor house and keep it in Your memory.

With the most distinguished esteem and gratitude, I sign myself Your Illustrious Lordship's

most humble Sr. ANNA M. ROSA GATTORNO

She asks for a subsidy for the school, already well established and attended, in the premises granted by the Town Council.

Most Illustrious Mayor,

1. I beg Your Most Illustrious Lordship to deign to grant the request of the undersigned.

2. The Town Council having kindly entrusted to the Daughters of Saint Anne a House in which a Boys' School is run, which today numbers 104 boys. By God's mercy they are making progress, to the edification of the public and the satisfaction of their parents.

3. I beg Your Excellent Lordship to share in so great a good by granting it some assistance, so that all applications for admission may be met.1

Confident of obtaining everything, I thank You in advance and remain with all esteem and respect Your Most Illustrious Lordship's

most humble Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The School's expenses were considerable, because besides general administration the pupils, all poor, had to be supplied with exercise books, books and everything else necessary.

The Parish Priest of Nizza will arrive in Piacenza, accompanying a postulant. She should prepare everything to receive him well. Various instructions concerning the Sisters and the girls in their care.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Yesterday I couldn't tell you anything more, and when I was on the train I read the letter from the Superior at Nizza,1 telling me that a small box containing Carlotta's watch was at the station.

2. She also told me that the Parish Priest of Nizza was accompanying a postulant to Piacenza. This assures me that he is coming to observe, and you know, after all those muddles, he will certainly come to see and question the postulant.2 Try to give him a very warm welcome and put him to sleep in the room called Father's room, and then open up the whole length of the guest quarters; and let the church be in very good order.

3. The schools and the girls must be clean and not shouting. For charity's sake, may he leave satisfied. I am sure he is coming to observe, so that he can say he has seen what the girls are like.

4. For my part, I would send Sr. A. Maddalena away, because she will always be a rotten apple and will infect all the others.3

5. I enclose a letter — you know for whom; you will have it tomorrow, and on Sunday send it at once by Giovanni with the usual instructions.4

6. Change at once the bed you put in the guest quarters, which

was meant for me; put the one we agreed; get your room ready, and likewise the bed upstairs in the postulants' dormitory for the one who is coming, so that she finds a clean dormitory with her bed made up. If you have none, you can put your own there; what do you say?5 If you have another, that will be better. I urge you to look for the house, but say nothing, fix nothing.6 I hope you have been to the Bishop and made my apologies.7

7. What I saw Sr. A. Eufemia doing with Sr. A. Cherubina was most indecent; it shocked me somewhat. My God! I did not believe such things could happen. What a pity, my dear daughter; our Holy Father was right when he insisted on this, and some said he had a suspicious mind;8 it seemed exaggerated to me too, but now I say he was right and that, alas, such things do happen. My dear, let us be watchful, for all that he has said and says are holy truths. Send for him; learn all his holy teachings from him, and you will be sure of going the right way.

8. For charity's sake, try to make arrangements for Father Agostino to be admitted to the baths. Try to recommend to the Bishop his protégée and this one and, if you can, go to Count Caracciolo and ask him to get two accepted, his protégée and another, and about the latter speak to the Doctor as to who needs it most. Likewise to Giacoboni for the sick girl...9

9. I will have a letter enclosed for Elena's father,10 and you try to make her understand that she should go home and that when she is cured she will find her place waiting. For charity's sake — with an amputation threatened, it would be a dreadful thing for us. Do what you can; besides, they would have to cut above the thigh. Tell that person; do everything to make her go; promise her that her place will always be there.11 Goodbye. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you and all the others.

1 On the train to Ferrara she read the letter from the Superior at Nizza, Sr. A.

Giacomina Schenardi, who told her to collect the little box with Carlotta's

watch, left behind in Nizza by mistake.

2 She also told her of the Parish Priest's arrival, warning her that he was coming to

see what the place was like. He would certainly want to see and question the postulant. She is Gia-

cinta Pizzorno, whom he had presented last January.

3 Certainly Sr. A. Maddalena Terzaghi, since the novitiate register shows

no other Sister of that name at that time.

4 Correspondence with Fr Tornatore was frequent.

5 You can put your own bed. To this extent she wanted her daughters de-

tached: ready to give up, if need be, even their bed! For they could consider

nothing their own. Cf. Rule 1869, Chap. 3, Poverty, par. 5.

6 Look for the house. She had asked her to look for a house in Piacenza for her

brother Emanuele. Cf. L 214, 1.

7 ...apologies for not having called on him during her short stay in Piacenza

after returning from Genoa. Cf. L 219, 1.

8 Concerning the vow of chastity, the Rule the Father had written and on

which he formed the Daughters of Saint Anne said among other things: "...It would be a fault most

abhorred if I saw that among you, out of levity or in play, you touched hands, shoul-

ders, etc.".

9 The Superior was to make the necessary applications to obtain free

sea-bathing treatment. She suggested asking the Bi-

shop to recommend Ermelinda Marchesi and Count Caracciolo Maria Massari, their re-

spective protégées, and for two others the doctor and Canon Pietro

Giacoboni respectively.

10 Elena Ferrari, a novice who was feared to need a leg

amputation. Cf. L 232, n. 3.

11 She asks that Fr Tornatore too reassure and comfort her.

She thanks him for his comforting letter. She has written a good part of the Constitutions, "drawing them from pure observance". It is a great consolation to her to have found observance and unity in the Communities. She has received requests for Sisters for two more hospitals, but has thought it best to defer them so as to concentrate on the Constitutions, which, once ready, she will deliver to the Holy Father and the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Forgive me for being slow to thank Your Excellency for the letter You kindly sent me, which contained words of comfort for me and removed many doubts that were troubling my mind. My poor health prevented me, as I wished to write in my own hand. May Your Excellency accept the warmest thanks of this humble servant, who hopes soon to express far better in person how great her gratitude is.1

2. I have already written a good portion of the Constitutions, keeping to Your obedience and drawing them from pure observance.2

3. Amid so many tribulations one consolation sustains me and gives me strength to overcome every adversity: in the round of the six Houses3 I made, I can assure You I found in all of them an observance and unity I could not wish greater. I bless God a thousand times for His work, and it confirms me ever more that I am the one who spoils everything and am truly good for nothing.4

4. I have been asked for two more Hospitals, but I thought it best

for now to defer any call, so as to deal only with the well-known matter, so important to me.5

5. As soon as the Rule has been revised by His Eminence,6 I shall go at once to Rome to lay it at the feet of His Holiness and of Your Excellency.

6. Deign to grant me Your Apostolic blessing, as, prostrate at Your feet, I remain Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most humble Servant Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 He had written to her on 6 April, comforting her and pointing out the grounds for con-

fidence, namely the good references from the Bishops about the Institute and the Holy Father's direct

interest; and urging her to persevere "in activity and fervour for

good". AFSA, 72, RdP 16.

2 ...drawing them from pure observance, that is, from the life of the Sisters, spir-

itually nourished by the charismatic food conveyed by the Rule of 1869 — by

"that" Rule which had been contested and set aside.

3 ...the six houses: two in Piacenza and those of Sampierdarena, Genoa, Nizza

Monferrato and Ferrara.

4 M. Rosa, in the charismatic tradition of so many Founders, is deeply con-

vinced that the work is the Lord's; she is the humble instrument, good for nothing, capable only

of spoiling everything.

5 The other two hospitals: at Ovada (AL) and Cortemaggiore (PC). She postponed

the openings to deal with the Rule.

6 By Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli Casoni.

She asks her to send the Rule urgently. She reassures her about the way she is acting and urges her to look after herself.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received your letter and cannot understand why you have not yet had Sr. A. Vincenza's letter telling you to send me the Rule at once — the version translated from the one in the church, which I must have left in the cupboard. If it isn't there, send me the Father's.1

2. For pity's sake, pack them securely; but I hope they are there and have the same cover as the first ones, you know, dark brown cardboard. You know; for charity's sake, look for them.

3. Send Maddalena away;2 the answer you gave Sr. A. Fortunata is right; I always reply like that to everyone. I do not want them meddling in anything without my permission.

4. I will write no more; take care, look after yourself, don't forget to take the pills, which will give you appetite and strength; it will all pass, but don't forget; in a word, look after yourself.

[Affectionate MOTHER ROSA]

1 She needed the manuscript of the Rule "translated", i.e. revised and touched up

by Fr Tornatore on the advice of friends in Rome. Cf. L 144, 6.

2 Cf. L 211, n. 3.

She need no longer look for a house for her mother. Various advice about the Sisters. The Superior is coming from Sampierdarena; for charity's sake, she must not find out that the Father has been forbidden to come to the Mother House. A parcel will arrive from Sampierdarena; she should keep its contents; she will also receive various items for the house from Ferrara. Every day, new sorrows. She should have them pray. The letters she sent her are for the Father. He should answer at once.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. First of all, I let you know that Mamma no longer wants the house in Piacenza, because Emanuele has already left for Milan; so thank Don Gaetano and tell him that for now nothing more will be done, since the invalid has gone to another City.1

2. As for Sr. A. Maddalena, I forgot to write yesterday that you can perfectly well put her in the school, as you wrote; as for Sr. A. Elena, stand firm; let it be so. Have the doctor tell Sr. A. Zaveria that she needs to go to her native air, and then stand firm and tell her that when she is better she will come back. Meanwhile send for her relatives to come and fetch her.2 As for Father Agostino [and] Teresina, listen: the Superior of S. P. D'Arena is to come to accompany Giovanna.3

3. For charity's sake, let nothing leak out about that person who no longer comes. For charity's sake, let no one say anything, no one. You must keep an eye on her and arrange for her to leave soon.4 Give her Teresina, but only if the Marchioness wishes it. Let us not get into trouble.5

4. A parcel will reach you from S. P. D'Arena containing a velvet cloth, that is, a large piece of red velvet. I want it well kept, for charity's sake, and also a yellow chasuble and pieces of white satin. Keep everything carefully, especially the velvet and the chasuble.

5. From here you will receive an embroidery frame with two blouse fronts begun. Put them in the guest room, and also a bonnet with a pattern drawn on it; you can have this copied and then put it away too. You will see how lovely they are. Keep them carefully, and keep that place well shut, so that no dust gets into those rooms. You will also receive a large lamp; have it hung in the middle of the guest-room hall — I think there is a ring in the ceiling — and hang it on a cord. You will also find some very pretty stoppers for the little bottles in your refectory. For charity's sake, don't let them get dirty; they have had them here for ages, and if you saw how well they look! Also some nice plates for the girls, for when we have boarders. Keep these carefully too, and other little things I am sure will please you. I am trying to collect all I can, including a small chest of drawers,6 which we don't have; put it in the guest quarters, down there in the middle by the door where the chair is. You will see, and arrange everything as you think best.

6. Yesterday your letter did not surprise me at all about that kind person's curiosity, but you answered the truth very well. My dear, so many sorrows; every day new ones come.

7. What news have you of Volpe? Has Landi done nothing more about S. Lazzaro?7 Let us hope; today the month of May has begun; keep it fervently, so that Mary may be moved to pity for the Daughters of her Mother. Pray, for pity's sake.

8. If you think fit to send that surplice8 with its pattern to be embroidered or copied, you can send it with the pieces of white satin that will reach you from S. P. D'Arena.

9. Those letters you sent me were for the Father, because he must answer them. Immediately, yes; for charity's sake, get them to him at once and tell him to reply at once.

10. My God, tribulations on every side; here too there is

a share. I really don't know where to turn for support [except] to the Heart of God, where I rest and leave you, calling myself ever yours, your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you and all the others.

1 Cf. L 211, 6. Don Gaetano Bersani had also undertaken it; a friend of Ales-

sandro, M. Rosa's son, he occasionally put him up during his stays

in Piacenza, usually in the holidays.

2 Maddalena Terzaghi was now behaving well; she was "on probation", so her dismissal

had been suspended. Sr. A. Zaveria Borella, owing to an illness incompatible

with religious life, had to return home and did in fact go back to her family.

3 The Mother wanted Fr Agostino Donadio to benefit from sea-bathing.

Likewise the girl Teresina; so she told her to speak of it to the Supe-

rior of the Sampierdarena House, Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, who would be going to

Piacenza to accompany Giovanna, the girl who was to return to her family

because she could not adapt to boarding-school life. Cf. L 154, n. 5; 174, n. 3.

4 Sr. A. Paola was a devoted spiritual daughter of Fr Tornatore. The Mother

does not want her to learn of his removal from the Institute.

5 Teresina was a girl under the protection of the Marchioness Marianna Anguissola.

6 Una comodina: a small chest of drawers.

7 Giovanni Battista Volpe Landi, lawyer, Town Councillor and Ad-

ministrator of the "Opera Pia Alberoni"; Marquis Alfonso Landi. Benefactors of the

Institute.

8 A white liturgical vestment with wide sleeves, reaching to the

knees, edged with lace.

She should send the manuscript of the Constitutions already asked for. She will have a visit from the Princess. She is grateful to the Lord that the Princess did not come on the day she was in Piacenza. She should send her the surplice. Patience is needed: 1872 holds her in chains; 1873 will not be so. Courage and patience are needed. She is exhausted by the labours and worries of the house.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I am sending you the enclosed letter; send it on to its destination if he does not come. I am in the greatest distress because you have still not sent me the manuscript Constitutions I asked for.1 I fear the letter has gone astray — one, two, three letters, all lost then! For pity's sake send them to me at once.

2. I rejoice at the consolation you will have on Wednesday with the Princess visiting you. How good God is! Listen, daughter, this time he truly heard me, that she should not come on the day I was in Piacenza. I confess that for fear she might come I had the shakes for two days.2 I don't know why; it even pains me; on hearing her name every nerve in me shudders. For my part I can assure you that I pray for her and wish her a thousand blessings from Heaven, but what can I do!!!

3. Let us leave these useless things and come to the substance,

which for us is the house. Today I will write to the Bishop.3 I hear that Providence is coming; let us hope and always trust in God. Whoever trusts in Him alone will have everything. For the rest, you have done well in all you write me.

4. Yesterday I received a letter from Don Gaetano. He says nothing about Alessandro's slap. I hope you sent him the letter. He tells me he will come to settle Carolina's affairs.4 Well, do as you think; that way you will learn. Take heart and you will see that God will help you in everything.

5. You have not given me the surplice;5 if I had it I would have it begun. Listen, wrap it with a band crosswise, you know, the way the sheets of the receipt books are sent, that is, just one of the smaller ones, and send it to me here.

6. I hear what that person told you about Maddalena;6 well, do as he said. Show the house to the Parish Priest of Nizza too, and let it be in order.7 I hear about Sr. A. of the Good Shepherd; her turn will come too; let us be patient, for 1872 holds me in chains, but 1873 will not be so.

7. I hope so; everyone's turn comes; patience is needed; it is the Saints who beat the wicked; courage,8 if we want to win the victory. My dear, here too there are crosses without equal. I am drained of strength, for I can say that the wheel of this work always desfa(?) me blows and never rest; what anxiety.9

8. I hope you receive this tomorrow; that person will be there; I hope he will read this too, since I have no more time to add a line to his... from yesterday to today in this house — that is, as regards temporal affairs — I can tell you there are some very ugly things. My God! Pray, pray.

I am your poor

MOTHER ROSA

2 Presumably her Russian friend Maria d'Annenkoff. She is a spiritual daughter

ed, upset and grieved at his "removal" from the Institute.

3 Cf. L 219.

4 Don Gaetano; cf. L 214, n. 1. Carolina: cf. L 187, 3.

She answers a query, instructing her not to give a novice a dress or any other black clothing.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Two lines in haste, in reply to yours about Sr. A. Maddalena's things. I tell you she must not take away anything black;2 if her parents sent it, that matters little; her parents had said they would give many other things that they never gave, so you see it comes to the same. I think we should be a little strict. If that person thinks fit, give this letter to the one who is going. Goodbye; I am your

poor MOTHER. I have received the Rule; all is well.3

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 Maddalena: cf. L 211, n. 3; 214, 2; 215, 6. ...anything black, i.e. garments of

black cloth (aprons of the postulant's uniform, black habit) — she was to give her

nothing.

3 Cf. L 213, 1; 215, 1.

She expresses satisfaction and approves all she has done. The lack of providence is felt in the Ferrara house too. She has been writing for hours; it is two in the morning. She will send the almost finished Constitutions to the Bishop next day. Once the debts are paid, she should see whether she can send her 100 francs. She should pray for the Delegate in Genoa, who is ill, and look after her own health.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Send this letter on to its destination at once. Today I received a long letter from you with much news of the house and the fine arrangements you have made. All is well.

2. I hope you received the iron bed they sent you from Nizza; put it in Carlotta's room. I think the guest quarters will be fine now; nothing seems to be missing.

3. Listen, as for knocking down the infirmary, I would leave it as it is, because if some girl were to die, or there were others ill, you see, we wouldn't know what to do.1 Let us leave it as it is, and when the Lord sends providence we will arrange things differently.

4. My dear, here we are without providence; unless God works a miracle, it is a serious matter; my brain is wilting.2

5. Do you know what time I am writing? It will soon be two after midnight; I am alone in my room and, unable to sleep, I am writing — with spectacles now, because I can no longer see — having been sitting writing since 7 this evening; apart from the time for the rosary, I have written all the while.

6. In those Constitutions the works of piety are missing; I have had to supply everything from memory; I have now finished writing them; tomorrow I send them to His Eminence.3

7. Have them pray, for charity's sake, for I need it badly; here everything is going very badly. I hope to return soon to Piacenza; I have not yet written to the Bishop, but I will tomorrow.

8. As for the postulants, I would do this: tell the Parish Priest that both should enter together, and if one does not stay, the other's dowry should be bound to make it good, so that it doesn't happen that once they have placed with us the one with nothing, the other never comes;4 be very careful; take the names of all of them and of the Parish Priest, so that if we have to write we know to whom to address the letters.

9. You wrote to me about the flats Don Gaetano has found, but you don't tell me the prices; but do you know what I did? I had Sr. A. Vincenza write to Don Gaetano.5

10. When the Lord sends you enough to pay the miller, see whether you could send me about a hundred francs. Pay your debts first and then send them.

11. Late last night I received a letter [saying] that the Superior in Genoa was ill.6 I leave you to imagine what a blow this was for me; this morning I had another saying she was a little better; an inflammation of the throat, from one moment to the next.

12. Listen, think about taking care of yourself, for charity's sake, because you see how quickly it happens? Only this old dog of a mother of yours has bones like old dogs that never die.

13. As soon as I can I will write to the two wretched ones, Sr. A. En and Sr. A. Chi.7 Have them pray for this good Delegate, that she may soon be up again. They should take care that the girls who go to Church do not get up to tricks instead of praying, and should send one older and one younger girl together.8 Goodbye. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you all.

1 ...knocking down the infirmary to carry out alterations did not

seem to her either advisable or urgent.

2 Cf. L 214, 10.

3 In those Constitutions, i.e. the manuscript copy she sent her (cf. L

213, n. 1). I have finished writing them; tomorrow I send them to His Eminence, i.e. Cardinal

Luigi Vannicelli.

4 Of the two postulants, one had no dowry. She suggests making clear to the

Parish Priest a precise condition: if one wished to return

home, the payment owed to the

Institute for the costs of the postulancy should be met from the other's dowry.

5 Cf. L 211, n. 6.

6 Sr. A. Serafina Lorenzi.

7 The two wretched ones. One of her rare expressions of blame. She uses it here

for these daughters of hers, of whom Sr. A. Francesca complained of some unknown fault,

since her letter has not survived.

8 ...not get up to tricks, i.e. not wander among the pews

rummaging or taking the Sisters' books.

Some instructions. She should let her know when the trunk has arrived... She need not bother to send vegetables or other produce, as there is no need. She should approach the Prefect about the lottery.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. The Superior wrote to you about the sack; well, send only one; say nothing about the other, keep it.

2. I hope you can do everything I had written to you before the 13th of this month; that way things will be better.

3. Around the fifteenth (15th) the Superior of S. P. D'Arena will come and take Teresina with her, if the Marchioness wishes.2 When you have received the trunk, which should be today, write to me alone how you found everything and what was in it. I am sorry about the stoppers, there were no others. If it arrived safely, I will send you another with some plates for the girls. When there are services and other things (which) will be dear(?) to you. Hang the lamp now.3

4. Don't bother about vegetables, for they have everything here. Though if you have some in the garden, fine, but not much, for it would spoil; likewise only one salame, for charity's sake, because I repeat they have plenty here.

5. Send this on to its destination at once.4

6. Go and see the Prefect to commend the lottery to him and at the same time to see whether he has any good news for you about

what he led us to hope for.5 You did well about Grandi; keep sending someone to see how his mother is.6 Tell the little girls I will write to them soon. Goodbye. I am your

Affectionate M. R. The Lord bless you

2 The Superior, Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, will come on 15 May and take the girl

3 Cf. L 214, 5.

4 Send the letter to the addressee, Fr Tornatore.

5 Cf. L 221.

6 Keep sending a sister to the house of Councillor Giuseppe

ter cf. L 206, n. 3.

TO MGR ANTONIO RANZA

Ferrara, 26 April 1872

She has finished rearranging the Rule, which Mgr Giordani found "to his liking". It will be revised by Cardinal Vannicelli and sent by him to the S. Congregation. She will give him a detailed report in person.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Not having had the good fortune to come and receive Your Apostolic blessing while I was in Piacenza and to thank You warmly for all You do and have done for the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, whose gratitude will not fail, in prayers or in deeds, and wishing to give You the liveliest proofs of it, I now take up my pen to let You know that the reason was my poor health, as I was obliged to get up from my bed to resume the journey to Ferrara.1

2. Last night I finished rearranging the Rule; this morning I am expecting His Eminence's Secretary to hand it to him.2 Yesterday I had the honour of a visit from Monsignor Giordani, Bishop of Philadelphia, who looked over what I have written and, as far as I could tell, seemed to like it.3

3. It will soon be revised by His Eminence, who has undertaken, as he told me, to send it to the Sacred Congregation.4

4. Meanwhile I shall return to Your Feet and give You a full and detailed report in person.

5. Grant me Your Apostolic blessing, which I humbly await, as I declare myself Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most humble Servant Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 She had asked the Superior of the Mother House to call on him to apo-

logize for the missed visit. Cf. L 211, 6.

2 The Secretary, Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist.

3 Mgr Giordani: cf. L 184, n. 2.

4 It will be revised by His Eminence Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli and sent by him

to the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars.

.

She has handed the manuscript of the Constitutions to Cardinal Vannicelli for revision and comments. She wishes to know whether the copy to be sent to the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars must be printed.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Forgive me if I trouble You again with my tiresome handwriting, availing myself of the permission Your Excellency gave me when I was there, allowing me to write to You whenever I needed.

2. Today I handed the manuscript of the Constitutions to His Eminence for him to make the necessary observations;1 I should like to know whether, to be submitted to the Sacred Congregation, it must be printed.

3. His Eminence will send it to Your Excellency himself, and I shall wait with the keenest desire for the longed-for moment of the Decree of Praise; then, as I told You once before, I shall have the good fortune to be at Your Feet to tell You all that weighs on my soul.

4. My health goes from bad to worse, and every day I see the blessed moment of my departure drawing nearer, always hoping first to leave the Lord's Work firmly established.2

5. Deign to bless me, and may Your blessing bring me the strength I so much need. Deign to accept my humble respects as I remain Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 Cf. L 219, 2-3.

2 She often expresses her conviction that death is near; before lea-

ving her Daughters she wants God's Work to have the solidity of the Church's

recognition.

She recalls an earlier request for a subsidy for the girls in their care and renews it, trusting in his kindness.

Your Excellency,

1. The Superior, whom I sent in my place to ask Your Excellency whether through You the Government had yet granted what You have so kindly pursued for our poor little girls, who are in extreme need, not having had the good fortune to find You at the Palace, I take the liberty of reminding You of the matter in writing, though I am sure Your noble heart has not forgotten it.

2. The need in which this house finds itself urges me to beg You earnestly, sure of finding in You a kind father1 who will not delay in taking it up, so that this house may soon be helped in its many needs.

3. If my request were not too bold, I would ask You for a line bringing me some comforting news amid the many adversities in which I find myself. Please accept, Your Excellency, my respects, as with the deepest esteem and respect I sign myself Your Excellency's

most humble Sr. ANNA M. G. R.

1 Prefect Binda esteemed the Mother Foundress and on various occasions showed kindness to her Institute.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

4. Yesterday I received letters from the Vernengo sisters; I enclose one here for the sick girl.6 I will say no more because my health is poor. Greet all the Sisters and Don Luigi for me, and believe me your very poor

My good Father Agostino,

1. I have received your letter telling me the paintings are finished and asking where to send them.1 I would like them all to go to Piacenza, but I was afraid that the one of the Holy Mother in which the painter will have included the Eternal Father2 might be taken from me and the other given me instead; I would be very sorry. But if you, Father Agostino, are sure this will not happen, then send them all together to Piacenza, to Countess Caracciolo.

2. You ask about this good Lady.3 I can tell you that as soon as I reached Piacenza I sent word to her, knowing she wanted to speak to me, and as I was too ill to go, she had to come to me, and she brought me the interest on the house, which falls due these days.4 I blessed God for it and this good Countess, praying that the Lord may fill her with the graces she desires.

3. What a weight she took off my mind! Believe me, good Father, my worries are immense and my little head can no longer bear them. You know well that nothing is given us here any more; so this poor house too is full of tribulations and left to Providence, where we thought there was support.5 My God!

4. Let us rejoice at the thought that our Eternal Father deigns to press his divine hand upon this unworthy servant of his... I bless him, and laying everything at his feet, most tranquil on the cross where I find myself, I rest happily.6

5. When I feel myself fainting, I put my lips to one of the divine fountains of my Crucified One to take a sip of refreshment. Having drunk of that Most Holy Blood, I need nothing more; glad and strong I return to my work, which I am so poor at perfecting; indeed, in all truth I find that I always spoil it.7

6. The prayers you wanted are being said, but of course, as mine are among them, everything goes wrong, as one sees happening in other things. Meanwhile I thank you infinitely for all you do and have always done for this poor work.

7. The Rule is finished and I have already handed it to His Eminence.8 Now let God act. I can assure you that man had no part in it, and so I hope that, if not this time then another, it will be crowned with approval. God grant that this unworthy servant of his may see it, for I am galloping towards the end, or at least towards an illness.9

8. How I suffer, my God! You alone know it!! Paradise, you are so far away that truly great efforts are needed to reach you, since one cannot go up by carriage. And you know that I cannot go on foot because of my weakness; so all that remains is toil, and it takes me long, and then I always find big stones, which are my infirmities, and when I stumble on them I have to stop and find strength, ways to appease divine justice, and ask it to help me tread them down.10

9. I find I have no more paper, so I must stop; so it will be at the end of my days: I shall still have so much to put right in my poor soul and no more time; I grow ever more wretched. Believe me yours in Jesus

most humble and obliged Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The paintings of Saint Anne and the Sacred Heart, which a nephew of Fr Agostino had

painted on commission from the Mother.

2 She would like them sent to Countess Caracciolo in Piacenza,

so that of the paintings of Saint Anne the one that also shows

the image of the Eternal Father may be kept for her.

3 The good lady is the Countess mentioned above: Isabella Caracciolo.

4 She brought me the interest, i.e. the sum equivalent to the interest the Mother

had to pay Signor Giulio Sforza Fogliani on the debt incurred in buying the Palazzo Dal Verme. Her gift was entered in the Alms Register on 18 April 72: L. 1,000 (one thousand).

5 Countess Trotti had stopped giving the subsidy. So that house too,

the only one with secure financial support, is, like the others, entirely

dependent on providence, but with the added difficulty that, being regarded locally

as the Countess's work, it was hard to find benefactors.

6 From the failure of human support and the growth of tribulations

springs filial abandonment to the Father, and peace floods her inmost being.

7 When I feel myself fainting... She now opens her heart to her friend, good Father

Agostino, and gives him a fragment of her intimacy with the Trinity, expressing her

existential attitude in her relationship with God through symbols and words of spare and

effective simplicity: the cross, the crucifix, the divine fountains: the tree of life and

the Man who redeemed life by the cross and the blood. That "blood", gift

of the Father's mercy, price of redemption, drink and nourishment, re-

conciliation and peace, she draws from the fountains: the pierced wounds. And having drunk that

most holy blood, re-created by the energy of the Spirit, glad and strong she returns to work, rea-

dy to give herself, opening spaces of humility to the overflowing love of God.

8 Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli.

9 Her inmost desire: to leave to the FSA, whom she feels she must soon for-

sake because of her precarious health, the Institute firmly established with the approval

of the Church.

10 Finally, with clear acceptance of her own existential reality, she sketches the

vision of an ascetic path involving toil and reparatory love. Appeas-

ing divine justice. The doctrine of reparatory love or "satisfaction"

to divine justice, deeply felt and widespread in the spirituality of her time, had

a strong influence on M. Rosa's "piety".

1. Ho ricevuto la sua ed avendo un ritaglio di tempo l'occupo a risponderle. Come vede dalla data, sono sempre in Ferrara, perché ancora non sono revisate le Regole.1

3. Ho pure scritto al Vescovo Vitelleschi per vedere se devo fare stampare prima d'inviarle alla Sacra Congregazione e desidererei sapere se ha ricevuta la mia lettera, e cosa mi comanda, se devo farle stampare oppure che Sua Eminenza le mandi così. 4. Ne può parlare un poco al Padre Angelini.4 Le dica perché mai risponde alle mie lettere; sono di già due che gliene inviai e mai mi risponde, è vero che non ne sono degna.
